changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
changes.change: For operations decision-makers at event-driven merchants: lead with the person, not the plan. 'A name, not a queue.' Introduce the named solutions engineer and account lead who will own the account and pick up on peak days, then show the escalation path. Bring the response-time tiers in only as backup detail, if at all.
changes.why: When the COO asked who her person was, we answered with the tiers and response times. She dismissed that as 'a queue with a faster timer', while the customer's own words were 'A name, not a queue.' and 'Someone who picks up.'

changes.change: For merchants whose revenue spikes on scheduled events: add a written peak-event runbook as a standard proof point and offer it before anyone asks. It is our plan for an 'on-sale morning' and covers who is watching, who you call, and what happens in the first minutes of a failure. Build it with a solutions engineer. It does not exist today.
changes.why: The decider asked to see on paper what we do on an on-sale morning. The rep said 'We don't have that as a thing' and that he could have built one with our solutions engineer but didn't.

changes.change: For COO and operations buyers after an incident: open with what happens when payments fail, not with uptime or load-test results. Use her framing: 'I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down.' Keep the technical proof (sandbox load test, docs, uptime history) for the technical team, as the entry ticket rather than the closing argument.
changes.why: The uptime and load-test story won over the CTO's team, but the decider gave it only 'good' and framed her purchase as what happens when it's down.

changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
changes.change: For peak-event buyers: replace logo proof with a reference customer who can describe who picked up during a live incident on a big event day, and offer the introduction proactively.
changes.why: The rep said 'I had logos. I didn't have a person.' Logo-style proof did not answer the decider's question of who responds.
